nameStory: The Carolina rose gets its name from the Carolinas, where early botanists first formally described this native beauty. But don't let the name fool you — this tough little rose actually grows wild throughout most of eastern North America! It's also called the pasture rose because it thrives in open grasslands where livestock graze.
description: Carolina rose is a low-growing wild rose that forms dense colonies through underground runners. This native shrub typically reaches 1-3 feet tall and spreads to create thorny thickets. Unlike garden roses, it has simple five-petaled pink flowers and produces small red fruits called rose hips. The stems are armed with straight, slender thorns that help distinguish it from many other wild roses.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic five-petaled pink flowers, usually 2-3 inches across, with a sweet, light fragrance and bright yellow centers packed with stamens

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-9 small, oval leaflets that have finely toothed edges and feel smooth to slightly fuzzy underneath

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading shrub that forms colonies through underground runners, rarely growing taller than 3 feet but spreading widely

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Straight, slender prickles scattered along green to reddish stems, less curved and hooked than many other wild roses

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round to egg-shaped red rose hips that persist into winter, about the size of a pea with dried sepals still attached at the tip

habitat: Carolina rose thrives in sunny, open areas throughout New England including meadows, prairies, old fields, roadsides, and woodland edges. It prefers well-drained soils but tolerates a wide range of conditions from sandy to clay. You'll often find it growing alongside other sun-loving natives like goldenrod, asters, and native grasses in disturbed or semi-wild areas.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late April to May, followed by flower buds that begin forming in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through July with fragrant pink flowers that attract bees and butterflies. Spent flowers begin developing into small green hips.
seasonality.fall: Rose hips ripen to bright red and leaves may turn yellow to reddish before dropping. The colorful hips become prominent as foliage fades.
seasonality.winter: Persistent red rose hips stand out against bare thorny stems, providing food for birds and winter identification clues.

funFact: Carolina rose is essentially nature's own ground cover system — a single plant can spread underground to create a colony covering several acres, with what looks like dozens of separate bushes actually being one massive connected organism!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other wild roses, especially swamp rose and Virginia rose. Carolina rose stays lower and spreads more aggressively than swamp rose, and has straighter thorns than the more curved prickles of Virginia rose. Remember: Carolina = low colonies with straight spines.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "Carolina" rose, this species actually has one of the widest ranges of any North American rose, growing from Canada to Florida and west to the Great Plains. Early settlers and Native Americans both used the vitamin C-rich rose hips for food and medicine.
compareHints: Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright. Its straight thorns help separate it from Virginia rose's curved prickles, and it lacks the distinctive wrinkled leaves of rugosa rose. Unlike the invasive multiflora rose, Carolina rose has larger flowers and grows much lower to the ground.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.
Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
